questions.q: In the opening simulation, payments loses 1 response in 10 and checkout retries. Why were ten customers charged twice?
questions.explain: A caller cannot tell a lost request from a lost response or a slow service: all three look like a timeout. Retrying a non-idempotent operation after a lost response repeats it. In a function call inside one process, this "maybe it happened" outcome does not exist.
options: The network delivered each request twice
When a response is lost the charge already happened, but the caller only sees a timeout, retries, and charges again
The payments service had a bug in its counter

questions.q: Which is a genuine strength of a monolith that microservices lose?
questions.explain: With one database, consistency across features is a transaction. With a database per service, the same guarantee needs a saga with compensations, and the data can disagree for a while.
options: Each part can be deployed on its own
One database transaction can cover the order, the stock and the payment record
Each part can use a different programming language
A crash in one feature cannot affect another

questions.q: What makes a monolith a "big ball of mud"?
questions.explain: Size and a single deploy are not the problem. Tangling is. A large monolith with enforced module boundaries stays changeable.
options: Missing boundaries: any code can import any other and every feature reads every table

questions.q: In a modular monolith, the orders module needs a book's price. Which is the right way to get it?
questions.explain: Each module owns its data and exposes a small public API. Reaching into internals or tables couples orders to the catalog's implementation and makes a later extraction painful.
options: Query the catalog's books table directly, since it is the same database
Call a function exported by catalog/index.ts, the catalog's public API
Copy the catalog's pricing code into orders

questions.q: What does a modular monolith not give you?
questions.explain: It is still one deployable and one process: modules ship together, and a memory leak in one affects all. It keeps transactions and simple operations, which is often the better trade.
options: Clear ownership of modules by teams
Independent deploys and fault isolation between modules

questions.q: A system has a "book service", a "customer service" and an "order service", each wrapping one table. Every page calls all three, and most features change two of them. What is this?
questions.explain: Entity services are split by noun, not by business capability, so every feature crosses them. They must all be up and often deployed together.
options: A distributed monolith: the costs of the network with the coupling of a monolith

questions.q: In the catalog, "book" means title and price; in shipping it means weight and size. What does a bounded context design do with this?
questions.explain: One giant shared model couples every context to every other. Separate models, connected by ids and events, let each context change on its own.
options: Makes one shared Book type with every field, used everywhere
Lets each context keep its own model of a book, with only the fields it needs, linked by id
Puts shipping and catalog in one service

questions.q: "An order must never be confirmed without its stock being reserved" must hold at all times. Where should order placement and stock reservation live?
questions.explain: Strong consistency is cheap inside one database and expensive across services. Draw boundaries so the rules that must always agree stay together.
options: In two separate services, synchronised by a nightly job
On the same side of a boundary, so one transaction covers both; otherwise accept a saga and a moment of inconsistency

questions.q: Which operation is naturally idempotent?
questions.explain: Setting a value to the same thing twice has the same effect as once. Adding, charging and sending all repeat their effect, so they need an idempotency key or a record of what was handled.

questions.q: A developer generates a new random idempotency key inside the retry loop, for each attempt. What happens?
questions.explain: The key must identify the operation, not the attempt: made once, before the first try, and reused on every retry.
options: It works the same as a key per operation
Each retry looks like a new operation to the server, so lost responses still lead to double charges
It is safer, because keys cannot be guessed

questions.q: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
questions.explain: Without jitter, 1,000 clients that failed at once come back at once, every time. Randomising the wait spreads them out, as the simulation's "same moment" counts showed.
options: So that many clients that failed together do not all retry at the same instant and overload the service again
Because exponential backoff alone never retries

questions.q: Which failure should a client generally not retry?
questions.explain: A 400 will fail the same way every time: retrying only adds load. Retry failures that may go away, a few times, and only for idempotent operations.
options: A timeout on an idempotent read
A 429 Too Many Requests, after its Retry-After
A 400 Bad Request saying the quantity is invalid

questions.q: In the outage simulation, the breaker and the plain retries confirmed the same 30 orders. What did the breaker improve?
questions.explain: A breaker cannot make a dead dependency work. It limits the cost of the outage: callers fail fast, and the dependency is not hammered while it recovers.
options: It made the payments service recover sooner
It turned 90 calls that each waited a full timeout into 5 trial calls and 29 immediate failures, sparing customers and the struggling service
Nothing; it is only useful in tests

questions.q: What happens in the breaker's half-open state?
questions.explain: After the pause, the breaker probes carefully. The outage log showed exactly that: half-open then open while payments was still down, half-open then closed once it recovered.
options: Half the calls go through, half fail
One trial call is allowed; success closes the breaker, failure opens it again
All calls go through, but with a shorter timeout
The breaker resets its failure count and stays open

questions.q: Which message is an event?
questions.explain: An event is a fact in the past tense, for zero or more subscribers, and cannot be refused. The others are commands: requests to one handler, which may fail or reject them.
options: charge-card with an amount and a key

questions.q: What is a real cost of an event-driven design?
questions.explain: Loose coupling means nobody's code lists the whole process. You gain independence and pay in visibility, which traces and good event documentation recover.
options: The steps of a business process are spread across subscriptions, so the flow is hard to see without tracing
Adding a subscriber requires changing the publisher

questions.q: A broker promises at-least-once delivery. What must consumers do?
questions.explain: Redelivery after a crash between "work done" and "acknowledged" produces duplicates. Acknowledging first would turn duplicates into lost messages instead.
options: Be idempotent, for example by recording handled message ids with the work
Process messages in a random order

questions.q: What problem does the transactional outbox solve?
questions.explain: The event is written in the same transaction as the order, so both exist or neither does. A relay publishes it later. It can publish twice, which idempotent consumers handle.
options: The order being saved but its event never published (or published but never saved) when the process dies between the two steps

questions.q: Right after Ada places an order, her "my orders" read model does not show it. Which fix fits CQRS best?
questions.explain: Read models are eventually consistent by design. Waiting for projections couples the write side to every reader again. Showing the command's own result covers the moment the user cares about.
options: Make every command wait until all projections have run
Return the new order's data from the command so the screen can show it immediately, and let the read model catch up
Remove the read model and query the write model's events on every page view

questions.q: When is full CQRS with separate read models most worth its cost?
questions.explain: Separate read models pay off when reads and writes differ strongly in shape or load. For simple forms, they add projections and lag for nothing.
options: A settings form that saves one row
A shop where checkout writes must be fast and a dashboard needs many aggregated views over the same orders
Any project with more than one table

questions.q: Which job should an API gateway not take on?
questions.explain: Business rules belong in the services that own them. A gateway that accumulates rules becomes a monolith in front of your services, and every team must change it.
options: Deciding whether an order qualifies for a discount

questions.q: Why must every service copy the incoming trace id into its outgoing calls and log lines?
questions.explain: Without a shared id, the logs of five services are five unrelated piles. With it, a trace tree and a log search show one request's whole journey.
options: So one customer request can be followed across all the processes it touched

questions.q: A call fails on attempts 1 and 2 and succeeds on attempt 3. What does this print?
questions.explain: Here the service did the work on every attempt: the timeouts were lost responses. Without an idempotency key, three calls mean three charges.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every call with order-7 after the first returns the saved reference and charges nothing. Only two distinct operations happened.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The wait doubles each attempt, starting from the base, and is capped at 1,000 ms so it never grows without bound. Real clients then add jitter to each wait.

questions.q: A breaker opens after 2 failures in a row and pauses 1,000 ms. What does this print?
questions.explain: The second failure opens the breaker at 100. At 200 the pause has not passed, so the call fails fast even though the service now works. At 1,200 the pause has passed: half-open, the trial succeeds, and the breaker closes.

questions.q: The gateway calls two services in parallel with Promise.all. Each "call" returns its simulated latency. What does this print?
questions.explain: Calls one after another take the sum of their latencies; calls in parallel take as long as the slowest one. That is why a gateway aggregating services fans out in parallel.

questions.q: The broker delivered msg-2 twice. What does this print?
questions.explain: The naive count sees every delivery. The idempotent one skips the id it has already handled, so it counts each message once.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The relay publishes only unsent rows and marks them sent, so running it again publishes nothing new. ord-3 goes out on the second run.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Between the command and the next projector run, the read model is behind by one order: that is eventual consistency. splice(0) empties the queue, so each event is projected once.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ord-1 takes 2 (3 left). ord-2 reserves 2, the charge fails, and the compensation gives them back (3 left). ord-3 wants 4 of 3: rejected. ord-4 takes 3 (0 left).

questions.q: Each network call costs 40 ms of simulated latency. What does this print?
questions.explain: One call per line is 5 calls; one per distinct book is 3; one batch call is 1. Chatty boundaries multiply latency and failure chances, which is why good service boundaries need few calls per request.

questions.q: Write handle(message) for the receipt consumer so that each message id sends at most one receipt, even when the broker delivers it again. The program should print receipts: 3 and skipped: 2.
questions.explain: The consumer records each handled id after doing the work. In production that record lives in the consumer's database, written in the same transaction as the work, so a crash cannot separate them.

questions.q: Write a CircuitBreaker with allows(now), succeeded() and failed(now): it opens after 3 failures in a row, stays open for 5,000 ms, then lets one trial through (half-open). The program should print closed closed open open half-open closed.
questions.explain: The third failure opens it at 200. At 3,000 the 5,000 ms pause has not passed; at 5,300 it has, so the breaker goes half-open, and the successful trial closes it. Passing now in keeps the breaker testable without waiting.
questions.expected: closed closed open open half-open closed

questions.q: Write relay(db, publish): publish every outbox row that is not sent, in order, and mark it sent only after publish succeeds. If publish throws, stop and leave that row unsent. The program should print published: evt-1, then published: evt-1,evt-2,evt-3.
questions.explain: Marking a row sent only after a successful publish means a broker outage delays events instead of losing them. The next relay run picks up where the last one stopped, in order.

questions.q: Write bookPage(bookId): get the book (required) and its reviews (optional) in parallel. If the reviews call rejects, still answer with reviews: "unavailable"; if the book call rejects, answer { status: 503 }. The program should print 200 4.5, then 200 unavailable, then 503.
questions.explain: Promise.allSettled waits for both calls and never rejects, so one failing call cannot throw away the other's result. The required dependency decides the status; the optional one only adds data when it is there.

questions.q: Write crossesBoundary(from, target) for a modular monolith: it returns true when target is in a different module under src/modules/ and is not that module's index.ts. The program should print false true false false.
questions.explain: Going through another module's index.ts, staying inside your own module, and using shared code outside the modules are all allowed. Reaching into another module's internal file is the one violation.

questions.q: A consumer crashes once while handling msg-2. What does this print?
questions.explain: Acknowledging first removes the message before the work is done, so the crash loses it: at-most-once. Acknowledging after the work means the message is still there after the crash and is delivered again: at-least-once, which is why consumers must tolerate duplicates.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each span is printed under its parent, one level deeper. Among the gateway's direct children, reviews took longest, and its own child shows why: the database behind it used 110 of its 125 ms.
options:
gateway 130
  catalog 40
  reviews 125
    reviews-db 110
slowest call: reviews

gateway 130
  catalog 40
  reviews 125
  reviews-db 110
slowest call: reviews

gateway 130
  catalog 40
  reviews 125
    reviews-db 110
slowest call: reviews-db

gateway 130
catalog 40
reviews 125
reviews-db 110
slowest call: gateway

questions.q: Write retryDelays(attempts, base, cap, random): for attempt n (from 1), the limit is min(cap, base * 2 ** (n - 1)) and the delay is Math.floor(random() * limit) (full jitter). With the fake random below, the program should print [ 50, 100, 300, 400 ].
questions.explain: The limits are 100, 200, 400 and 800; the fake random picks a fraction of each. Taking random as a parameter is the same trick as the Clock port: the function stays deterministic under test.

questions.q: Write bestSellers(events), a projection: sum the copies per title over order.placed events, ignore order.cancelled for this exercise, and return the titles sorted by copies, most first, as "title: copies". The program should print [ 'Purple Hibiscus: 5', 'Things Fall Apart: 3' ].
questions.explain: A projection is a fold over events into a shape one screen needs. Because it can be rebuilt from the events at any time, you can add new read models later without touching the write side.

questions.q: Write placeOrder(id, quantity, pay) as a saga: reserve stock (reject if not enough), then call pay(); if it returns false, release the stock. Return "confirmed", "rejected" or "compensated". The program should print confirmed compensated rejected and then stock: 1.
questions.explain: ord-1 takes 3 (1 left). ord-2 takes 1, the payment fails, and the compensation returns it (1 left). ord-3 needs 2: rejected. Each step that changes something has an undo that runs when a later step fails.
